subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 7-year-old boy falls off a swing and sustains a bending injury to his forearm. Radiographs show an incomplete fracture extending only partway through the width of the bone, with the cortex broken on the convex side while the concave side remains intact. The bone appears bent like a green twig.
question: Which of the following is the most likely fracture type?

options.text: Torus (buckle) fracture
Complete transverse fracture
Greenstick fracture
Comminuted fracture
Avulsion fracture

explanation_correct: A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture that extends partway through the width of a bone following bending stress. The bone fails on the tension side while the compression side remains intact, so the bone is bent like a green twig. This is a classic pediatric fracture pattern because children's bones are more pliable.

explanation_incorrect.A: A torus fracture results from axial force with buckling on the compression side and an intact tension side, not a bending force with failure on the tension side.
explanation_incorrect.B: A complete transverse fracture extends through the entire width of the bone rather than only partway through as described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: A comminuted fracture is characterized by multiple bone fragments, which are not present in this incomplete, bent fracture.
explanation_incorrect.E: An avulsion fracture occurs when a tendon or ligament pulls off a fragment of bone at its insertion, not from bending of the shaft.

educationalObjective: A greenstick fracture is an incomplete pediatric fracture from bending stress with failure on the tension side and an intact compression side.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 5-year-old child falls onto an outstretched hand with the force directed axially through the forearm. Radiographs show the cortex buckled and fractured on the concave compression side of the distal radius, while the convex tension side remains solid. There is no displacement.
question: Which of the following best describes this fracture?

options.text: Greenstick fracture with tension-side failure
Salter-Harris type I physeal fracture
Spiral fracture from rotational stress
Torus (buckle) fracture
Displaced greenstick fracture

explanation_correct: A torus (buckle) fracture occurs when axial force is applied to immature bone, causing the cortex to buckle and fracture on the compression (concave) side while the tension (convex) side remains intact. This is a stable, usually nondisplaced pediatric fracture, contrasting with the greenstick fracture in which the tension side fails.

explanation_incorrect.A: A greenstick fracture fails on the tension side with the compression side intact, the opposite of the buckling on the concave side described here.
explanation_incorrect.B: A Salter-Harris type I fracture is a physeal separation through the growth plate without a metallic cortical buckle, which is not described in this child.
explanation_incorrect.C: A spiral fracture results from rotational force and has a helical fracture line rather than a compression-side cortical buckle from axial loading.
explanation_incorrect.E: A displaced greenstick fracture would fail on the tension side and show displacement, whereas this fracture is a nondisplaced compression-side buckle.

educationalObjective: A torus (buckle) fracture is an axial-loading injury of immature bone with buckling on the compression side and an intact tension side.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A medical student is comparing two pediatric forearm fractures. In the first, a bending force produces a fracture through only one cortex with the bone bent like a twig. In the second, an axial force produces a cortical buckle. She is asked which side of the bone fails in the first, greenstick, injury.
question: Which side of the bone fails in a greenstick fracture?

options.text: The compression side fails while the tension side remains intact
Both the tension and compression sides fail completely
Only the periosteum fails while the cortex remains intact
The compression side buckles while the tension side fractures
The tension side fails while the compression side remains intact

explanation_correct: In a greenstick fracture, bending stress causes the bone to fail on the tension (convex) side, while the compression (concave) side remains intact, so the bone bends like a green twig. In a torus fracture the situation is reversed: axial force causes buckling on the compression side with the tension side intact. Distinguishing the two sides is a classic teaching point.

explanation_incorrect.A: Compression-side failure with an intact tension side describes a torus (buckle) fracture, not a greenstick fracture.
explanation_incorrect.B: Both sides failing completely would be a complete fracture, not an incomplete greenstick fracture.
explanation_incorrect.C: A greenstick fracture involves cortical failure on one side, not isolated periosteal failure with an intact cortex.
explanation_incorrect.D: Compression-side buckling with tension-side fracture combines features incorrectly; torus has buckling with an intact tension side, and greenstick has tension-side failure without buckling.

educationalObjective: Greenstick fractures fail on the tension side with an intact compression side, whereas torus fractures buckle on the compression side.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A newborn has disproportionate short limbs and a relatively large head. His father is 48 years old. Genetic testing is performed, and the counselor explains that this is the most common cause of short-limbed dwarfism, with more than 85% of cases arising sporadically and a dominant inheritance pattern with full penetrance.
question: Which of the following best describes the underlying genetic abnormality?

options.text: Activating FGFR3 mutation with autosomal dominant inheritance
Loss-of-function FGFR3 mutation with autosomal recessive inheritance
Autosomal recessive type II collagen mutation
X-linked recessive mutation affecting growth plate chondrocytes
Trisomy 21 with generalized growth retardation

explanation_correct: Achondroplasia results from constitutive activation of fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), which inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and impairs endochondral longitudinal growth. More than 85% of mutations occur sporadically, it is autosomal dominant with full penetrance, homozygosity is lethal, and it is associated with increased paternal age. It is the most common cause of short-limbed dwarfism.

explanation_incorrect.B: Achondroplasia is a gain-of-function FGFR3 disorder with autosomal dominant inheritance, not a loss-of-function recessive condition.
explanation_incorrect.C: Type II collagen mutations cause chondrodysplasias such as achondrogenesis, not the FGFR3-related short-limb dwarfism described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Achondroplasia is autosomal dominant and not X-linked, and paternal age rather than sex-linked inheritance is the recognized association.
explanation_incorrect.E: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome with characteristic features and not the disproportionate rhizomelic shortening and large head of achondroplasia.

educationalObjective: Achondroplasia is a gain-of-function FGFR3 mutation, autosomal dominant with paternal age association and lethal homozygosity.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: An infant with achondroplasia has markedly shortened limbs but a head that appears large relative to the body. Neurologic examination is normal and intelligence is unaffected. The clinician explains that the disparity reflects the different mechanisms of bone formation in the limbs versus the skull.
question: Which of the following best explains the relatively large head in this child?

options.text: Membranous ossification is also inhibited, but cranial sutures close late
Endochondral ossification is impaired while membranous ossification is unaffected
Increased intracranial pressure drives compensatory skull overgrowth
Hydrocephalus from aqueductal stenosis enlarges the cranium
Vitamin D resistance increases mineralization of the cranial bones

explanation_correct: In achondroplasia, failure of endochondral ossification impairs longitudinal bone growth and produces short limbs. Membranous ossification is unaffected, so the skull develops normally and appears large relative to the shortened limbs. Constitutive FGFR3 activation inhibits chondrocyte proliferation, which selectively affects the growth plate-dependent endochondral skeleton.

explanation_incorrect.A: Membranous ossification is unaffected in achondroplasia; it is endochondral ossification that fails, so the head size is relatively preserved rather than overgrown.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chronic intracranial pressure is not the mechanism of the large head; the cranial vault is normal in size and the appearance results from limb shortening.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hydrocephalus is not a typical feature of achondroplasia and would not explain the disproportionate limb shortening with a normal-appearing skull.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vitamin D resistance is not part of achondroplasia and would produce rachitic changes rather than isolated failure of endochondral growth.

educationalObjective: Achondroplasia impairs endochondral ossification causing short limbs, while unaffected membranous ossification yields a relatively large head.
